In addition, the Strong Vocational Interest Inventory, Bell Adjustment Inventory, and Wrenn Study Habits Schedule are administered. The results are made available to individual students, departments, deans, and class advisers within a week for individual, class, and curriculum planning. During the second semester of sophomore year a battery of achievement tests are given to aid in further course plans for major concentration and elective work. The last battery given at the beginning of the second term of senior year includes achievement tests and the repetition of the Strong Vocational Interest Inventory to aid in vocational choice and educational plans for graduate study. Success of the program is dependent upon the training of advisers or counselors, and the giving of sufficient time for individual analysis, discussion, and decision. The program has developed a keen interest on the part of members of the faculty in problems of testing and individual student guidance. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Dunlap, J. W.

title: Is high school adequate preparation for college?
abstract: College students and graduates reported in a questionnaire on the adequacy of high-school preparation for the first year of college. 12.6% considered it adequate. 25.9% thought they had been given an insufficient foundation of factual knowledge, especially in English and foreign languages. 22.2% said they had not been trained in good study habits. 20.7% felt they had not been given sufficient opportunity to develop self-discipline and initiative in acquiring information. 15.6% complained they had not been trained sufficiently in clear self-expression, written or verbal. 14.8% emphasized lack of training in rapid and wide reading. Smaller numbers felt the chief inadequacy to be in too little training in reflective thinking, use of libraries, and taking of examinations. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2018 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Barnes, R. A.

title: The use of hypnosis in a college counseling service
abstract: Various procedures are presented in which use of hypnosis is a valuable asset in treatment of student problems at a college counseling service, especially in cases of anxiety manifestations, and difficulties concerning learning processes and study habits. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Summo, Anthony J.; Rouke, Fabian L.

title: Long-term effects of behavioral counseling
abstract: ATTEMPTED TO DETERMINE EFFECTIVENESS OF BEHAVIORAL COUNSELING IN MODIFYING STUDY BEHAVIOR, AND THE EXTENT TO WHICH MODIFIED BEHAVIOR GENERALIZED TO A NONCOUNSELING SETTING. 684 COLLEGE STUDENTS WERE SELECTED AT RANDOM FROM 1500 VOLUNTEERS FOR A PROJECT TO IMPROVE STUDY HABITS. SS WERE ASSIGNED RANDOMLY TO 4 CONDITIONS, 2 EXPERIMENTAL AND 2 CONTROL. REINFORCEMENT COUNSELING WAS THE PRIMARY INDEPENDENT VARIABLE, WITH RESPONSE CONTINGENT REINFORCEMENT USED WITH SS IN SMALL COUNSELING GROUPS. CRITERION MEASURES ADMINISTERED IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWING TREATMENT AND 3 MO. LATER REVEALED SIGNIFICANT DIFFERENCES BETWEEN EXPERIMENTAL AND CONTROL GROUPS ON BOTH TESTINGS. MODIFIED BEHAVIOR GENERALIZED TO THE NONCOUNSELING SETTING AND RESPONSE STRENGTH PERSISTED. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2017 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Ryan, T. Antoinette

title: Cognitive styles, study habits and faculty choice
abstract: PREDICTIVE STUDIES OF UNIVERSITY STUDENTS' PERFORMANCE HAVE NOT BEEN MARKEDLY SUCCESSFUL BECAUSE SUCH WORK HAS MADE SIMPLE AND INAPPROPRIATE ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT THE PSYCHOLOGY OF COMPLEX HUMAN BEHAVIOR. RECENT WORK SUGGESTS THAT CERTAIN PERSONALITY AND COGNITIVE STYLE VARIABLES MAY BE HIGHLY RELEVANT TO THE PREDICTIVE SITUATION. ON THE BASIS OF AN INFORMATION PROCESSING MODEL, AN APPROACH IS SUGGESTED IN WHICH THE STUDENT'S STUDY HABITS ARE USED TO ASSESS THE RELEVANT COGNITIVE STYLE TYPE VARIABLES. COMPLEXES OF STUDY HABITS DIFFERENTIATING BETWEEN FACULTIES WERE ISOLATED, THESE COMPLEXES BEING A FUNCTION OF THE STUDENT'S PERSONALITY AND OF HIS PREVIOUS TRAINING. IT IS EXPECTED THAT PREDICTIONS ON THE BASIS OF THESE 'STUDY STYLE' COMPLEXES WOULD BE MORE SUCCESSFUL THAN THOSE DERIVED FROM IQ OR MATRICULATION AGGREGATES ALONE. (PAPER READ AT AUSTRALIAN PSYCHOLOGICAL SOCIETY ANNUAL CONFERENCE, 1967.) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2017 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Biggs, J. B.

title: Correlation of personality traits with success in scientific decision-making
abstract: Students were trained in decision-making skills in a 10-mo Wayland Baptist College Decision-Making Project. At the end of the project 20 students wrote decision statements which were ranked by judges for successful use of decision-making skills. Rankings for strength in 59 personality traits were available from personality profiles prepared for each student at the beginning of the project. The following personality traits were found to be significantly related to success in scientific decision making: mathematical ability, practical problem-solving, rote memory, concentration, range of interests, curiosity, good imagination, maturity, and purposiveness. Interest in school and study habits were also positively related. These traits, found in successful decision makers, suggest a student who is eager to learn. They support like findings in other Wayland Project studies. The implication here is that training in the attitude, a genuine desire to know the truth, would be a key catalyzer as an integral part of future courses in decision-making. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Barber, Lucie W.

title: Abilities, transfer, and information retrieval in verbal learning
abstract: Suggests that cognitive strategies, 'functioning as higher order responses to the characteristics of a learning task, provide a mechanism of transfer from abilities to learning performance.' Cluster size was varied to examine the choices of strategies of graduates, undergraduates, and 1 faculty member (total N = 120). Hypotheses concerning differences: (1) among treatment group centroids for response and strategy measures, (2) in dependence of measured abilities and response measures and strategy choice, and (3) in relationships of specific abilities to response measures were tested and the results discussed. (41 ref.) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Frederiksen, Carl H.

title: Controlling classical conditioning with sentence structure
abstract: Randomly assigned 64 undergraduates to 1 of 2 learning strategies for associating visually presented male names with orally presented evaluative words. The contiguity treatment produced attitude changes in the direction of the associated evaluative words. The negative statement treatment stopped the conditioning effect and in 2 cases significantly reversed the direction of attitude change. It is concluded that sentence structure can dramatically alter the role that contiguity plays in verbal attitudinal learning. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Walton, Dan R.

title: Desensitization and study-skills training as treatment for two types of test-anxious students
abstract: Compared the effectiveness of systematic desensitization and training in efficient study methods for reducing test anxiety among a total of 194 undergraduates with high emotionality or worry scores on Osterhouse's Inventory of Test Anxiety. It was hypothesized that Ss reporting high levels of emotional arousal during examinations would benefit more from treatment by desensitization, while Ss reporting high levels of cognitive worry about their test performance would benefit more from training in study skills. This hypothesis was not supported. Desensitization Ss reported significantly less anxiety during a final examination than did no-contact controls. Controls received significantly higher examination scores than did study-skills Ss, primarily as the result of improved academic performance by controls reporting high levels of emotional arousal. Desensitization offered more promise as a treatment method for test anxiety than training in study skills. (23 ref.) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Osterhouse, Robert A.

title: Cognitive strategies, experimenter modeling, and expectation in the attenuation of pain
abstract: Obtained verbal reports of pain from 120 female undergraduates during a base-level pretest and also during a posttest conducted under 1 of several experimental treatments. The pain stimulus was a heavy weight applied to a finger for 2 min. During the posttest, Ss who had been asked to utilize cognitive strategies for reducing pain (i.e., to imagine pleasant events or to imagine the finger as insensitive) showed a reduction in pain as compared to uninstructed control Ss. Ss led to expect a reduction in pain, but not provided with cognitive strategies, also showed reduced pain during the posttest compared to controls, but the reduction was smaller than for Ss using cognitive strategies. An E modeling procedure, used with half of the Ss under each experimental treatment, was effective in reducing verbal reports of pain only for Ss with high pretest levels who were asked to imagine pleasant events. (29 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Chaves, John F.; Barber, Theodore X.

title: The influence of specific stimulus information on the concept learning process
abstract: Performed 2 concept learning experiments, each with 120 undergraduates, in which the stimulus dimensions were applicable to persons. In Exp I, conditions used either well-known pictorial exemplars of descriptive combinations only for those stimuli carrying key solution information, pictorial exemplars only for stimuli not containing such information, pictorial exemplars for all stimuli, or no pictorial exemplars. In addition, problems varied with respect to number of stimuli needed to specify the solution. Solution ease was greater the fewer the stimuli necessary to identify the concept. Exp II compared 2 groups on a transfer task in which no pictures were presented. The groups received initial training on problems with or without pictorial exemplars of key stimuli. Evidence indicates some negative transfer for the 1st group relative to the 2nd group, suggesting that specific stimulus information may enter into learning strategies. Data of the experiment suggest that a modification of current hypothesis theory is called for. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Nahinsky, Irwin D.; Oeschger, David E.

title: The use of hypnosis in a course to increase academic and test-taking skills
abstract: Studied the effects of hypnosis on academic and test-taking skills. In contrast with previous research with inadequate experimental design and statistical methodology, an experimental research design with appropriate statistical analysis was used. Ss were 93 college students, and treatment was administered by prerecorded cassette tapes over a 4-wk period during regular class time. Tapes consisted of hypnotic and waking suggestions related to course content and general academic skills. Hypnotic and waking suggestions did not facilitate academic skill learning significantly more than class curriculum alone. Pre–post comparisons did indicate significant improvement by all groups on reading, writing, study skills, and spelling variables. (German, French, & Spanish summaries) (17 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Cole, Randy D.

title: Effects of instructions, biofeedback, reward, and cognitive mediation on the control of heart rate and the application of that control in a stressful situation
abstract: 90 male and 90 female undergraduates were instructed to try to either increase or decrease their heart rate (HR) with or without the use of biofeedback, and with or without the promise of money for successful performance (no-treatment Ss were given no instructions, no biofeedback, and no promise of reward). When simply instructed to do so, Ss could increase but not decrease their HR relative to no treatment controls, the promise of money for good performance aided Ss in increasing but not decreasing HR, and biofeedback did not aid Ss in either increasing or decreasing HR. Various cognitive strategies employed by Ss in controlling their HR are discussed. In a 2nd phase of the experiment, Ss in a stress condition were told that they would receive a series of painful electric shocks, whereas Ss in a no-stress condition were not told about shocks. All Ss were instructed to try to decrease their HR during the 'shock' period. HR and self report data revealed that (a) the manipulation was successful in increasing stress, and (b) previous training in decreasing HR, with or without biofeedback, did not aid Ss in decreasing their HR in the face of the stress. (27 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Bennett, David H.; Holmes, David S.; Frost, Randy O.

title: Which students benefit from self-paced mastery instruction and why
abstract: Based on an attribute-by-treatment interaction paradigm, the determinants of 217 female college students' achievement were compared under conventional and self-paced mastery examination schedules in an anatomy and physiology course. Measures of general scholastic ability (e.g., Minnesota Scholastic Aptitude Test) did not interact with method, but prior preparation in science did. Ss with less science preparation showed greater achievement under self-paced mastery testing than their counterparts under conventional testing. This compensation was explained when study habits were explored. Under self-paced testing, study time was inversely related to amount of science background. Self-pacing Ss with less background reported greater textbook usage and indicated that unit test results aided in planning study effort. No such relationships were found for Ss in the conventional course. (38 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Stinard, Thomas A.; Dolphin, Warren D.

title: Group vicarious desensitization of test anxiety
abstract: Examined whether vicarious desensitization, using videotapes and a small group format, could be used as a treatment for test anxiety. 43 test anxious college students were administered the Test Anxiety Inventory and the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory. Ss received either vicarious desensitization, study skills training, or both treatments; there was also a no-treatment control condition. Self-report measures indicated that vicarious desensitization resulted in lower test and trait anxiety than study-skills training alone or no treatment. Academic performance measures, obtained posttreatment and at a 3-mo follow-up, indicated no differential effectiveness. (10 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Altmaier, Elizabeth M.; Woodward, Margaret

title: Variations in cognitive behavior modification for test anxiety
abstract: D. Meichenbaum's (see record [rid]1973-20259-001[/rid]) cognitive behavior modification treatment for test anxiety consists of a cognitive (insight) and a behavioral (modified desensitization) component. In the present experiment with 45 undergraduates, variations on the insight and the behavioral component of the program were examined. Ss were randomly assigned to 1 of 3 treatment or 2 control groups. One group received Meichenbaum's cognitive behavior modification treatment. For a 2nd group, Meichenbaum's desensitization component was retained, but the insight component was altered by substituting specific statements concerning pressure. In the 3rd group, Meichenbaum's insight component was retained and test-taking practice was substituted for the desensitization component. All treatment groups also received study-skills training. Multiple self-report and performance measures of anxiety were obtained. The combination of Meichenbaum's insight component with test-taking practice was most effective in increasing facilitating anxiety and decreasing debilitating anxiety. (22 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: McCordick, Sharon M.; Kaplan, Robert M.; Smith, Shirley; Finn, Mary E.

title: Cognitive strategies and running performance: An exploratory study
abstract: Examined the cognitive strategy use of novice runners and the effects of training to adopt either associative or dissociative cognitive strategies on the performance of new runners. 31 college students in fitness classes were randomly assigned to an associative group, a dissociative group, or a relaxation control group. Before, during, and after 5 weeks of strategy training, Ss competed in a 1½-mi run. Analyses revealed that all runners used increasingly more associative cognitive strategies over the training period. However, those runners who employed relatively more dissociative cognitive strategies demonstrated a greater reduction in running time over trials relative to students who reported using more associative strategies. The interaction between cognitive strategy use and physical skills is discussed. (5 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Okwumabua, Theresa M.; Meyers, Andrew W.; Schleser, Robert; Cooke, Chris J.

title: The effectiveness of mastery learning strategies in undergraduate education courses
abstract: Studied the effectiveness of a group-based teacher-paced mastery learning instructional model in undergraduate education courses. Two of 6 sections of a required education course on teaching handicapped children in regular classrooms were taught using mastery learning strategies. The instructors of these 2 classes developed a series of formative tests with accompanying feedback and corrective activities and administered these measures following instruction on each unit in the course. Corrective work was completed outside of class by Ss who did not attain 90% mastery on the formative tests. Although the course content, sequence of topics, activities, and group-based instruction were identical in all sections, only in the 2 mastery sections were there regular checks on learning progress coupled with corrective activities. Data were gathered from 197 advanced undergraduate students. Results indicate that even after controlling for demographic and affective variables, Ss in mastery learning sections scored higher on a common final examination, attained higher course grades, and were absent less often than Ss in sections taught by more conventional methods. Implications for teacher training and college-level instruction are discussed. (19 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Clark, Charlotte R.; Guskey, Thomas R.; Benninga, Jacques S.

title: Effects of systematic desensitization and self-control treatments in test-anxiety reduction programs
abstract: Assigned 28 test-anxious college students, screened on the basis of their scores on the Suinn Test Anxiety Behavior Scale (STABS) and the Survey of Study Habits and Attitudes, to systematic desensitization (SD), self-control desensitization (SCD), or a delayed treatment control group. SCD and SD Ss were administered the STABS, the Trait scale of the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and the Tennessee Self-Concept Scale pretest, and all 3 groups completed the measures postintervention. Controls completed the SCD treatment at the time the 2 treatment groups were tested at 4-wk follow-up. Results indicate that SD and SCD did not differ in effectiveness in reducing self-reported test anxiety at posttest or follow-up. Continued reduction in trait anxiety from posttest to follow-up was found for both groups, and both groups showed an improvement in GPA. The control group showed improved self-concept following delayed treatment. (23 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Knapp, Samuel; Mierzwa, John A.

title: Comparison of three cognitive strategies in altering pain behaviors on a cold pressor task
abstract: Examined the efficacy of 3 cognitive strategies for coping with pain in a cold-water pressor task in a sample of 35 undergraduates. Ss were pretested and then randomly assigned to 1 of 3 treatment conditions (paradoxical intention, rational self-statement, or self-observation) or to an expectancy control group. Following training in the respective cognitive strategies, all groups were given a posttest in the cold-water pressor to determine the effectiveness of the treatment. Pain thresholds, tolerances, and discomfort ratings were recorded for subjects in each condition. No differences were found between the paradoxical intention or rational self-statement groups and the expectancy control on any of the pain measures. The self-observation treatment condition, however, had significantly higher pain tolerance scores than the expectancy control group. Findings are attributed to the Ss' dissociating the sensory aspects of the pain experience from the anxiety when focusing upon the coldness and wetness of the cold water. (9 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Gilligan, Robert M.; Ascher, L. Michael; Wolper, Jeffery; Bochachevsky, Chrystyna

title: Individuelle Unterschiede bei der willentlichen Kontrolle des Herzschlags = Individual differences in voluntary heart rate control
abstract: 50 male university students were instructed to control their heart rates and were given feedback during 2 training sessions, each of which consisted of 4 8-min trials in which Ss were to increase or decrease their heart rates. Personality measures included the State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, Rotter's Internal–External Locus of Control Scale, the Repression-Sensitization Scale, and the Eysenck Personality Inventory. Physiological measures included respiration rate, forearm flexor EMG, and nonspecific GSR frequency. Multivariate analysis resulted in distinct clusters of physiological patterns, personality dimensions, and cognitive strategies. Findings support the idea that equivocal results of mediational research with operant heart-rate conditioning are due largely to variations in individual responding, personality differences, and variable cognitive activity. (German abstract) (53 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Fenz, Walter D.; Pye, David; Favaro, Paul

title: Serial position phenomena: Training and retrieval effects
abstract: Studied the retrieval shift by which primacy items are usually among the first to be reported on the initial list in successive free recall, and recency items then take over and are reported first on later lists. This shift was studied in 4 experiments using a total of 143 undergraduates as Ss. Exp I had 30 Ss practice on 5 free recall lists over 3 trials. Results support the hypothesis that primacy reduction is caused by proactive interference rather than by the primacy to recency report shift. In Exp II, a case study of 5 Ss examined over a period of 3 mo, only slight improvement on single-trials lists with extensive training was found. However, when 52 naive Ss were given 4 successive trials with the same type of cue-conflict list in Exp III, prominent practice effects were easily demonstrated. Results confirm the assumption that repeated presentations of items located in middle list positions may counteract the privilege of primacy and recency positions. When repetitions were made within contracting and expanding lists in Exp IV, the results proved that active anchoring, making itself visible as primacy effects, is feasible with contracting lists but difficult with expanding lists. Active performance of list learning strategies generally resulted in primacy effects; whereas passive shortcut procedures, in learning and retrieval of information, produced recency effects. A problem-solving theory is presented as an alternative to information-processing models of serial learning and memory. (51 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Helstrup, Tore

title: Discovery and expository learning compared: Their effects on independent and dependent students
abstract: Compared the effects of discovery-learning (DL) and exposition-application (EA) teaching formats on students with independent and dependent learning styles in an introductory college chemistry course. It is noted that the DL method encourages students to generate conclusions inductively from ambiguous materials, whereas, in the EA format, the structure of the material is presented at the start to help guide student learning. It was predicted that Ss with an independent learning style would learn more productively in the freedom of the DL situation, while the structure of the EA format was predicted to be more beneficial to dependent learners. On a posttest immediately following instructions, the DL format was found to be superior for both groups of Ss. The superiority was markedly greater for the independent Ss, so that the predicted aptitude–treatment interaction was also present: Independent Ss outperformed dependent Ss in the DL condition, while the reverse was true in the EA setting. (41 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Andrews, John D.

title: Computer-presented organizational/memory aids as instruction for solving Pico-fomi problems
abstract: Computer-generated organizational/memory charts were used as tools to help students develop their own learning strategies and to provide extensive feedback for complete use of these tools. The 104 undergraduate Ss attempted to solve 8 Pico-fomi problems under experimental treatment followed by a 2nd set of 8 under optional use of the tools. The treatments were verbal or matrix organizational/memory charts and learner control (LC) or computer control (CC) of use of the charts. Results show that while some Ss maintained performance when CC was withdrawn, others succeeded only as long as they were under CC. Similarly, although some Ss succeeded under the LC condition, others did not. It is suggested that control of use of charts should be adapted to learners' knowledge and problem-solving styles. (8 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Steinberg, Esther R.; Baskin, A. B.; Matthews, Terri D.

title: Hypnotic analgesia and stress inoculation in the reduction of pain
abstract: Investigated the influence of hypnotic ability on 3 methods of reducing cold-pressor pain. Following a baseline immersion, 30 high- and 30 low-hypnotizable undergraduates were randomly assigned to 1 of 3 treatment groups: stress inoculation training, stress inoculation training defined as hypnosis, or hypnotic analgesia. Analysis of pain reports indicated a significant hypnotic ability×treatment interaction. Among Ss receiving hypnotic analgesia, high-hypnotizables reported significantly less intense pain than lows. There was no differential response for high- and low-hypnotizable Ss receiving stress inoculation training, whether or not it was defined as hypnotic. Moreover, Ss in the stress inoculation condition (whether or not defined as hypnosis) reported using cognitive strategies to reduce pain, whereas this was not the case for Ss in the hypnotic analgesia condition. The present findings seem inconsistent with the social psychological account of hypnosis and are discussed from a dissociation perspective, which views hypnosis as involving changes in the way information is processed. (56 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Miller, Mary E.; Bowers, Kenneth S.

title: Learning strategies: An instructional alternative for low-achieving adolescents
abstract: Describes a set of task-specific learning strategies designed by the University of Kansas Institute for Research in Learning Disabilities as an instructional alternative for learning disabled (LD) students. These learning strategies teach students how to learn so that they can cope more effectively with the increased curriculum demands as they move from elementary to secondary schools. The rationales underlying the learning strategies approach for adolescents are reviewed. Three factors that have influenced the way in which learning strategies have been designed for and taught to LD adolescents are identified, including the long history of failure they bring to remedial situations, their minimal motivation for participation in academic instruction, and time constraints. Strategies developed include matching instruction with curriculum demand, using structured teaching techniques, deliberately promoting generalization, using scope and sequence in teaching, and maximizing student involvement. All of the studies to date indicate that once training in a strategy has been implemented, the students show marked gains that are highly correlated with the level of staff training. (39 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Deshler, Donald D.; Schumaker, Jean B.

title: A social-cognitive skills approach to the successful modification of hypnotic susceptibility
abstract: 120 undergraduates who were low and medium in hypnotic susceptibility were administered cognitive strategy and instructional set information and practiced responding to test suggestions to enhance susceptibility. Those in 1 modification treatment received this information both from the experimenter and by observing a videotaped female who responded successfully to suggestions and reported on the cognitive strategies she used to do so. Those in a 2nd modification treatment received the information and practice but were not exposed to the model. Low and medium susceptibles in a 3rd condition (practice alone) received a hypnotic induction procedure and practice suggestions but neither modification information nor modeling. No-treatment controls performed a filler task. All Ss were posttested on 2 susceptibility scales. Results show that information plus modeling produced significantly greater increments on all objective and subjective indices of susceptibility on both posttests than did practice-alone or control treatments. Susceptibility increments in the information without model treatment always fell between those of the model and practice-alone treatments. In the modeling treatment, over half of the initial low susceptibles and over two-thirds of the initial medium susceptibles scored as high susceptibles on both posttests. Findings provide strong support for a social-cognitive skill formulation of hypnotic susceptibility. (49 ref) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Gorassini, Donald R.; Spanos, Nicholas P.

title: Differences in learning processes and academic achievement
abstract: Examined (1) the relationships among the scales of the Inventory of Learning Processes by R. R. Schmeck (see record [rid]1979-00139-001[/rid]), (2) differences between high and low academic achievers, and (3) differences between deep and shallow processors on learning strategies and academic achievement for 158 undergraduates. Significant correlations among the scales were noted; significant differences between high and low academic achievers appeared on Deep Processing and Fact Retention scales; and differences between deep and shallow processors were noted on Elaborative Processing, Fact Retention, Methodical Study scales, and grade point average (GPA). It is suggested that students should be offered strategy-training programs. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Gadzella, Bernadette M.; Ginther, Dean W.; Williamson, J. David

title: Self-report and psychophysiological effects of five pain-coping strategies
abstract: 100 nulliparous female undergraduates were randomly assigned to a series of 10 treatment groups that comprised a variety of cognitive-behavioral pain-coping strategies as part of a labor preparation analog. The efficacy of these treatments was subsequently assessed during a 1-hr session involving 20 80-sec exposures to a laboratory pain stimulus patterned to resemble labor contractions. Dependent variables included self-reported pain, systolic and diastolic blood pressure, frontalis electromyogram (EMG), and heart rate. One of the cognitive strategies—sensory transformation—had a significant effect on self-reported pain; analyses conducted on the other 5 dependent variables failed to show significant treatment effects. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Geden, Elizabeth A.; Beck, Niels C.; Hauge, Gregory; Pohlman, Susan

title: Predicting compliance with home relaxation training
abstract: Examined the ability of self-prediction, self-motivation, a stress profile, and a state-trait personality measure to predict compliance with home relaxation training. Although several significant correlations were obtained between these dimensions and the practice of relaxation at home, only achievement orientation and self-motivation predicted adherence to the relaxation regimen for 27 undergraduates. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Flanders, Philip; McNamara, J. Regis

title: Perceptions of racism by Black medical students attending White medical schools
abstract: Interviewed 31 Black medical students attending 5 White medical schools concerning racism experienced in high school, college, and medical school. Over half the Ss reported experiences of racism in high school and college, and 29 of 31 reported such experiences during medical training from both White patients and physicians. Cited reactions were anger and shock, and in some instances study habits were affected positively and negatively. Ss reported periods of active avoidance and mistrust of White students. Emphasis was placed on mutual support among minority students, and the importance of the faculty and minority office for coping with the stresses associated with racism. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Bullock, Samuel C.; Houston, Earline

title: Self-motivation vs previous grades as predictors of success in counsellor training
abstract: Compared level of self-motivation, as measured by questionnaire, to previous grades in psychology and nonpsychology courses as predictor variables of success in an introductory counselor training course. Written, practical, and combined assessments of 30 Australian graduate students in the course were used as the criterion variables. Findings show that motivation to succeed was the most effective predictor variable. The selection of students to undertake counselor training is discussed. (French abstract) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Sharpley, Christopher F.; Pain, Michelle D.

title: Hypnosis, relaxation and analgesia suggestions for the reduction of reported pain in high- and low-suggestible subjects
abstract: 24 high- and 32 low-suggestible undergraduates from New Zealand were administered 1 of 4 analgesic treatments (hypnosis plus analgesia suggestion, relaxation plus analgesia suggestion, analgesia suggestion alone, no treatment) prior to a painful arm immersion in ice water. Ss reported on the ratio of pain experienced in the 2nd immersion relative to a pretreatment immersion and the cognitive strategies they used. Analgesia suggestions following hypnosis were superior to waking analgesic suggestions in reducing reported pain, but did not differ in their effect from analgesic suggestions following relaxation. High-suggestible Ss reported greater pain reduction than low-suggestibles following analgesic suggestion. Ss who worried about or exaggerated the unpleasantness of the immersions reported more pain than those who did not. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2017 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Tripp, E. Gail; Marks, David

title: Diferencias individuales en auto-control dentro del paradigma de tolerancia a la estimulación aversiva = Individual differences in self-control within the tolerance to aversive stimulation paradigm
abstract: Studied the role of individual differences in self-control in pain tolerance, comparing the cognitive strategies used by high and low self-control Ss. Human subjects: 80 female Spanish adults (mean age 23 yrs) (university students in psychology courses) (high self-control). 80 female Spanish adults (mean age 23 yrs) (university students in psychology courses) (low self-control). The Ss were assigned to treatment cells of a 2 by 4 factorial design, were given 1 of 4 types of cognitive instruction, and underwent a cold pressor test. Tests used: The Self-Control Scale by M. Rosenbaum (1980). (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Ruiz, M. Angeles; Avia, M. Dolores

title: The effects of an active development of the mental model in the training process: Experimental results in a word processing system
abstract: Compared 3 training programs for a word processing system: (1) a sequential program, which taught low-level skills and which did not help the user actively to develop a mental model; (2) a hierarchical program, which provided an explicit and integrated conceptual model of the system to the user; and (3) a program in which the users were asked to develop hypotheses on the functioning of the software and in which they were encouraged to use an active and exploratory approach. Ss were 15 college students. From an action theory viewpoint it was hypothesized that the 3rd group would be superior to the 1st group. In 2 training sessions, this was shown to be the case for several performance criteria. An interindividual difference variable to measure the individual learning style was used, giving results that could be interpreted in a similar way to the experimental results. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Frese, Michael; Albrecht, Karen; Altmann, Alexandra; Lang, Jutta; Papstein, Patrizia V.; Peyerl, Reinhard; Prümper, Jochen; Schulte-Göcking, Heike; Wankmüller, Isabell; Wendel, Rigas

title: Mental imagery training: Effects on running speed performance
abstract: Assessed the effects of single and combined cognitive strategies on long-distance running speeds over a 12-wk training period in 36 male and 29 female college students (aged 17–22 yrs). Ss were assigned to 1 of 4 different conditions (skills, results, results/skills, or control). Running speeds were superior over the initial 4 wks of training for the internal (skills) imagery group relative to controls; no significant differences were evident for the motivational, psyching-up (results) group, or the combined results/skills group. All groups showed the same level of improvement by the end of the 12 wks of training. Gender differences and anxiety/stress effects were also noted. (French, Spanish, German & Italian abstracts) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Burhans, Rollins S.; Richman, Charles L.; Bergey, Donald B.

title: Maximizing athletic performance in endurance events: A comparison of cognitive strategies
abstract: Contrasted 2 cognitive strategies commonly used by endurance athletes: external focus and dissociation. In Exp 1, 20 physical education college students rode stationary bikes for 30 min at a fixed rate while distracted in one condition or attending to internal state in the other condition. In Exp 2, 12 male college track team members ran 1 mile at their normal training pace in each of 3 imagery conditions. Ss concentrated on a pleasant scene unrelated to running (dissociation), features of the environment (external focus), or heard a brief essay (no imagery). Dependent measures included perceived time and effort and actual performance times. Results show that performance increased with distraction, with external focus providing more distraction than dissociation. Findings replicate J. W. Pennebaker and J. M. Lightner's (see record [rid]1981-22664-001[/rid]) research with joggers and cyclists. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Padgett, Vernon R.; Hill, Angela K.

title: Academic underachievement
abstract: academic difficulties are sensitive indicators of students' general psychological well-being, and cannot be abstracted from the context of their level of development, adaptive style, psychodynamic conflicts, social functioning, family expectations, and situational demands / a clinically sophisticated assessment can aid the decision about the most appropriate approach to choose from the diverse array of responses available in college counseling or treatment centers three types and numerous subtypes of interventions can be identified / individual didactic and cognitive approaches, such as peer tutoring and study skills counseling, are particularly for students who have specific and remediable academic problems / group interventions, such as issue-focused groups, workshops, and courses in study strategies, create an atmosphere of joint noncompetitive learning, mutual support, increased interpersonal self-confidence, promotion of maturation, and beneficial exchange of information / individual psychological treatment-counseling or psychotherapy—is appropriate for the resolution of situational challenges or interactional or intrapsychic conflict (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Ducey, Charles P.

title: Content area reading and study
abstract: problems associated with separating the process of learning how to read and study from the task of learning subject matter content were reviewed / noted that despite the plethora of books and articles published on the topic of 'content area reading,' many elementary, secondary, and college teachers still teach separate reading and study skills courses rather than integrating these skills with the teaching of subject matter content a recommended solution to this problem was to teach students a study system that fosters independent learning / a theory was reviewed to explain why teaching a study system is likely to result in increased student learning of content / suggestions for teaching a study system were outlined selective attention theory (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Santeusanio, Richard P.

title: Transfer effects of prior knowledge and use of graphic organizers on college developmental readers' summarization and comprehension of expository text
abstract: Investigated the transfer effects of training in the use of graphic organizers and summary writing on college developmental readers' recognition of the compare/contrast text structure. 52 college freshmen required to take a developmental reading/study skills course were assigned to an experimental or control group. Training was centered on 8 scientific expository texts, each of which had a compare/contrast internal organization. Experimental Ss received instruction that included explicit rules and modeling for constructing graphic organizers and writing summaries. Results of posttests show that comprehension scores of the experimental and control groups were not significantly different. However, experimental Ss were able to transfer their training to real-world textbook materials. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Balajthy, Ernest; Weisberg, Renee

title: Mood and self-motivation in successful and unsuccessful female rowers
abstract: Assessed mood state using the Profile of Mood States and self-motivation (SMI) in 84 female undergraduates vying for a position on a collegiate rowing team. 44 Ss also completed a standardized rowing ergometer task. Mood state was assessed 3 more times with 22 Ss who adhered to training throughout the entire season. No differences in baseline mood state were observed between the 62 dropouts and the adherers. Dropouts possessed significantly lower SMI and took longer to complete the rowing task than did adherers. Near the end of the season, some Ss were chosen to compete in regional competition (i.e., successful adherers). Initial SMI and ergometer performance did not differ significantly between successful and unsuccessful adherers. Global mood disturbance increased during training season, particularly for unsuccessful adherers. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2017 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Raglin, John S.; Morgan, William P.; Luchsinger, Amy E.

title: Learning style and the efficacy of computer training methods
abstract: Administered the Kolb Learning Style Inventory (D. A. Kolb, 1976) to 80 undergraduate novice computer users. Using 1 of 2 training methods based on different conceptual models, Ss were trained to use an electronic mail filing system. Performance accuracy was assessed on 3 experimental tasks. As hypothesized, Ss with the Converger learning style had highest overall performance. However, a significant interaction between training approach and learning style was also hypothesized and supported, indicating that the efficacy of training models depends on a fit with learning style. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Sein, Maung K.; Robey, Daniel

title: Effects of teaching generative vocabulary strategies in the college developmental reading program
abstract: Compared the relative effectiveness of 4 learning strategies on the initial acquisition and retention of new vocabulary in 80 undergraduates enrolled in a developmental reading course. Three generative strategies (vocabulary log, imagery, and suggestology), as well as a traditional approach, were used in 7-wk instructional treatments. An analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) procedure was employed to determine vocabulary growth at weekly intervals during the treatment and at 3 wks following treatment. No significant differences were noted between groups for either immediate learning or delayed recall. All groups showed significant short- and long-term growth. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Stahl, Norman A.; Brozo, William G.; Smith, Brenda D.; Henk, William A.

title: Counseling the college-bound student with a learning disability
abstract: Discusses specific strategies to help high school counselors (HSCs) in dealing with college-bound learning disabled (LD) adolescents. These strategies include (1) career counseling, (2) awareness of college programs and requirements, (3) fitting the student to the college, (4) fostering the development of organizational and study skills, (5) assisting in the development of compensatory strategies, and (6) facilitating social adjustment. HSCs should be aware of the factors that increase the probability of success for college-bound LD students. The transition from the structured, relatively controlled environment of high school to the less structured environment of college, it is concluded, can be particularly difficult for LD students. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Skinner, Michael E.; Schenck, Susan J.

title: Estrategias de aprendizaje, especialidad y rendimiento académico = Learning strategies, fields of study, and academic performance
abstract: Studied common dimensions of 50 different learning strategies (LSTs) and the relationship among differences in the use of learning strategies, major field of study, and scholastic performance. Human subjects: 543 Spanish adults (university students). Ss included students in physics, chemistry, technical architecture, medicine, psychology, law, teacher training, philosophy, and history; and translators and interpreters. Information on personal and sociodemographic factors and on learning strategies was obtained via administration of a questionnaire. Ss were asked to read a list of learning strategies and indicate the degree to which they used each strategy. The grade average for each student was obtained from student records. A multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and other statistical tests were used. (English abstract) Educational. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Cano, F.; Justicia, F.

title: Reading problems: Consultation and remediation
abstract: In the past few years, Instructional Consultation has emerged as a major new model of service delivery in the schools. This model of teacher/specialist collaboration has been shown to be particularly effective in helping the increasing numbers of children identified with reading problems. Designed to help both school psychologists and reading specialists effectively assume the consultation role, this volume provides an overview of reading problems while serving as a guide to effective practice. The book outlines the principles of consultation, and discusses the psychology of the reading process, reading instruction, and the nature of reading disabilities. Diagnostic procedures and a variety of intervention strategies that are in use for improving word recognition skills, vocabulary, comprehension, and metacognition are described in detail. A section on improving writing and study skills at the college level is also included. The use of mini-computers as instructional aids is discussed, and a brief survey of software programs designed to assist reading instruction is presented. Appendices contain informal assessment tools, an evaluation of basal reader series, and reviews of standardized reading tests. Also included are typical questions asked by parents and teachers with suggested answers. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Aaron, P. G.; Joshi, R. Malatesha

title: Feminist perspectives in therapy: An empowerment model for women
abstract: This book addresses core issues in counseling women within the context of two major theoretical positions and a sample of client concerns. The book will be useful both to beginning graduate students who desire an introduction to counseling women, as well as to more advanced and professional clinicians. Advanced professionals may want to discover and integrate these emerging approaches into their therapeutic repertoire, or may selectively adapt text materials for workshops and continuing education training. Each chapter contains a self-assessment pretest on knowledge or attitudes, an introductory overview, a chapter summary, and self-awareness activities. The self-assessment and self-awareness exercises are excellent learning strategies for students, and contribute to the usefulness of this book as a classroom or continuing education text. The underlying theme of the text emphasizes that effective counseling with women clients requires an awareness of personal stereotypes about this client population, an understanding of self in relation to women, and a sensitivity to the special psychological and social environments within which women's development takes place. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Worell, Judith; Remer, Pam

title: Death in the school community: A handbook for counselors, teachers, and administrators
abstract: When a death occurs in the school community, all students, teachers, and staff are affected to some degree. In the case of a violent or sudden death, a school community may be deeply affected. . . . Because the number of violent deaths involving children of all ages is growing, it is important that schools plan carefully how they will respond. The purpose of this book, 'Death in the School Community: A Handbook for Counselors, Teachers, and Administrators,' is to assist schools to plan and respond effectively to a death. 'Death in the School Community' will interest and provide useful information for school counselors, teachers, administrators, school safety officers, and crisis intervention specialists. . . . This publication, with its discussions of research and theory, reports of effective practices, outlines for counseling groups, practical planning guides, and case studies, explains in detail how to plan for and respond to deaths that affect a school community. Readers will learn the importance of establishing a plan and learning strategies and techniques to facilitate healthy resolution of students' grief before a tragic event occurs. The focus of this publication is on death in elementary and secondary schools. It addresses specific needs of school personnel; however, much of the information can be adapted for use in other settings and with college or older students. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Oates, Martha D.

title: Cooperation: A community college and a rehabilitation center
abstract: Describes the development and 2-yr implementation of a cooperative agreement between DeKalb College and the Georgia Sensory Rehabilitation Center intended to assist hearing-impaired students. A cooperative memorandum was developed which identified 5 areas of service: placement, preparation, coping skills, community services, and both personal social adjustment counseling and vocational counseling. The agreement was initiated due to the increase in applicants with potential to prepare for developmental studies. These needs included assessment, academic upgrading, vocational information, and study skills improvement. Fostering self-esteem was critical. With emphasis on academic preparation, students were able to continue in the program with minimal attrition. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Johnson-Sligar, Theresa; Sligar, Steven R.

title: Cognitive therapy with inpatients: Developing a cognitive milieu
abstract: 'Cognitive Therapy with Inpatients,' the first volume to describe the development of a 'cognitive milieu,' is a practical manual that presents effective cognitive strategies and procedures for short-term psychiatric hospitalization. Designed as a treatment guide for all professionals who work in hospital settings, this unique volume is a valuable resource for psychiatrists, psychologists, social workers, occupational therapists, and nurses. It also serves as a text for graduate courses in cognitive therapy, psychiatry residency training programs, psychology doctoral programs, and graduate programs in psychiatric nursing. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Wright, Jesse H.; Thase, Michael E.; Beck, Aaron T.; Ludgate, John W.

title: The effect of self-motivation on headache reduction through biofeedback training
abstract: Investigated the effects of self-motivation in biofeedback training on reduction of headache frequency, severity, and reliance on headache medication use in 49 college students who experienced at least 3 headaches per week. Ss' scores on a self-motivation inventory were used for assignment into groups of low and high self-motivation. Both prior to and after 8 wks of biofeedback training, Ss recorded over a 15-day period the number of headaches experienced, severity level, and amount of medication taken. During training they were given instruction on increasing skin temperature by using biofeedback instruments. High self-motivation Ss were better able to decrease their level of headache severity. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Thackwray-Emmerson, Danette

title: Establishing educational partnerships with strategic interventions through video-mediated staff development
abstract: Describes a video-mediated program produced by university faculty to provide classroom teachers with the skills to teach learning strategies to students at risk. Strategies for Efficient Learning and Functioning (SELF) is intended to help inefficient learners assimilate strategies and metacognitive behaviors that will enable them to meet the demands of mainstream classrooms. Two strategies that are accompanied by videos are writing paragraphs and comprehending reading. Anecdotal comments from teachers who have completed the SELF training indicate satisfaction, and nearly half of the approximately 150 Ss have developed successful programs in their own schools. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Welch, Marshall

title: The influence of ability on analogical transfer
abstract: In Exp 1, 16 gifted and 20 average undergraduates were presented with a story analogy before an attempt to solve a radiation problem. Gifted Ss did not produce significantly more dispersion solutions (enhanced by the analogy) than average Ss. In Exp 2, 15 gifted and 15 average students from the Exp 1 sample solved 6 problems while thinking aloud. Gifted Ss used significantly more analogies (most often association analogies, but sometimes transformation analogies) than average Ss. In Exp 3, 8 average university students were trained in metacognition problem solving. They solved 3 problems before and after training, while thinking aloud. Training affected problem solving performance but not analogical reasoning. In Exp 4, 21 university students were given training geared more toward improving analogical reasoning abilities. Effects of this training were less impressive than effects of training in other strategies. (Italian abstract) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Jaušovec, Norbert

title: The impact of trainee characteristics on the family therapy skill acquisition of novice therapists
abstract: Examined the impact of the initial phase of family therapy (FT) training on 99 novice family therapists' skill acquisition. The influence of 4 trainee characteristics on skill acquisition was also investigated. Ss, who were drawn from 5 graduate training programs in counselor education or marriage and FT, completed 3 assessment instruments. Results revealed significant changes from pre- to posttesting in FT skills in 3 out of 4 areas. Changes in trainee skill levels were significantly predicted only by the extent of initial knowledge of FT. The trainee characteristics of prior individual or FT work experience, prior individual or FT training, or trainee learning style were not significant predictors of trainee's skill gains. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2017 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Goodman, Rita L.; Amatea, Ellen S.

title: Estrategias de aprendizaje y rendimiento académico = Learning strategies and academic performance
abstract: Studied psychometric characteristics of the Spanish version of an instrument for assessing the association between learning strategies, academic performance, and field of specialization among students in a teacher training program. Human Ss: 439 normal Spanish adults (university students). Information on use of learning strategies, academic performance, and field of specialization was obtained by questionnaire. The reliability, external validity, structural validity, and subscale validity of the instrument were determined. Test used: The Learning Strategies Inventory (R.R. Schmeck et al, 1977). An ANOVA, factorial analysis, correlational analysis, and other statistical tests were used. (English abstract) (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Castejon, J. L.; Montañès, J.; Garcia Correa, A.

title: Problem-based learning in dietetic education: A descriptive and evaluative case study and an analytical comparison with a lecture-based method
abstract: Problem-based learning (PBL), a case-driven, student-centered educational approach, has been shown to foster critical thinking, problem solving, and self-directed learning skills, and enhance knowledge base acquisition and retention. PBL has been recommended by dietetic educators, but has not been formally evaluated. The purpose of this study was to describe dietetic student response to a PBL format. Subjects were 32 undergraduate dietetic students (UDS) in a lifecycle nutrition class and 52 dietetic interns (DI) from five Midwestern intern sites. The research design was a descriptive and evaluative case study with an embedded experimental design (generalized randomized block factorial). The UDS were randomly assigned to study the infant and elderly units using PBL or a lecture-based method. Data from the UDS and DI were obtained with ten instruments that assessed knowledge, attitude, learning style, sensation seeking traits, and opinions. Findings from the experimental component were analyzed with a three-way analysis of variance. PBL students were more apt to use articles, books, and professionals to study than lecture notes. Interpretation of knowledge acquisition results was confounded by significant treatment interactions: Only PBL UDS who started with the elderly unit scored higher than LBC UDS. Tenets that PBL enhances retention, self-directed learning skills, and motivation level were not supported for the UDS. PBL use was associated with a change in motivating factors from self and achievement to the group and knowledge. Use of memorization decreased for PBL UDS and DI; reflective thinking increased for PBL UDS, but confidence in problem solving skills did not increase. Self-directed learning skills and confidence in problem solving skills increased for DI; DI reported less frustration and stress with PBL than the UDS, rating PBL more positively on the Positive Learning Experience Scale and expressing a high desire to experience PBL again and incorporate th (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Bayard, Barbara Lohse

title: Differences between EDPSY 100 and non-EDPSY 100 students on study skills as measured by the learning and study strategies inventory (LASSI)
abstract: In light of the continued need to help students who are having academic troubles in higher education, the primary purpose of this research study was to examine the differences in study skills between those college students enrolled in EDPSY 100 and those not enrolled in EDPSY 100. The overall goal of the 'Study Skills for College Students' course is to help students acquire the knowledge and skills they need to take more responsibility for their own learning. In addition, this research study assessed which study strategies the EDPSY 100 students learned during a 15-week study skills course. The study skills' scores came from a self-reported measure, the Learning and Study Strategies Inventory (LASSI), which was developed by Weinstein, Palmer, and Schulte (1987). For this study, 105 EDPSY 100 students (49 females, 56 males) and 114 non-EDPSY 100 students (94 females, 20 males) were asked to complete the following: a consent form, pre-LASSI, post-LASSI, and demographic questionnaire. A multivariate analysis of variance was used to determine significant gains in learning strategies for EDPSY 100 students following a 15-week course in study skills training. The initial findings of the analysis revealed that the EDPSY 100 and non-EDPSY 100 students significantly differed. However, there were no significant differences between the two groups in their use of study strategies after the EDPSY 100 students completed a one-semester study skills course. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Arthur, Angela Deeann

title: Expert calibration of performance
abstract: The purpose of this study was to address competing hypotheses regarding the effects of domain specific prior knowledge on learners' abilities to effectively monitor performance. University students either expert or novice in the domain of probability predicted their performance prior to both a reading assessment and three probability assessments. After answering items, learners also rated the accuracy of their responses. Independent t-test procedures indicated that predictions, performance and post-test accuracy ratings did not differ between groups on the reading assessment. On the probability assessment, repeated measures ANOVA procedures indicated significant main effects for both group and difficulty level for predictions, performance and post-test accuracy ratings. These findings indicate, contrary to previous research, that domain-specific prior knowledge assists learners in effective monitoring of performance. Additional findings indicated no gender differences in ability to predict or to calibrate performance. Further findings suggested the possibility of across-task monitoring skills in some learners. These findings are of particular interest to those interested in training learners in metacognitive skills. Implications for instruction were presented. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Dennison, Rayne Sperling

title: The effects of scripted cooperative learning on academic performance of Black South African college students
abstract: This study investigated the effects of study condition (cooperative and individual) and script type (high, low, and no script) on academic performance of 195 Black South African male and female first year college students. The study also investigated the relationship among demographic factors, cultural variables and performance under the different experimental conditions. The relationship between task liking as measured by the evaluative questionnaire and post-test performance was also investigated in this study. This study was conducted in four phases. During phase 1 males and females were independently assigned the 12 experimental conditions. Participants were also administered a pre-test. During phase 2 the participants were administered a battery of questionnaires designed to assess: (1) demographic background experiences, and (2) communal orientation (both the Social Outlook Scale, and the Social Orientation Index). Phase 3 was devoted to training the participants in various learning strategies. Session 1 of phase 4 involved learning a different passage using the same instructions provided during phase 3. During session 2 participants took a post-test, and completed the evaluative questionnaire. The following hypotheses were tested: (1) cooperative dyads would perform better than participants learning alone, (2) the three script types would differ such that participants using high scripts would perform better than those assigned to the low script and the no conditions, (3) females learning as cooperative dyads would perform better than males assigned to the same condition, (4) significant positive correlations would be found among post-test scores, demographic variables, cultural variables, and the evaluative items for participants learning as cooperative dyads, (5) participants learning as cooperative dyads would like studying the passages better than participants learning alone. The results indicated that cooperative dyads performed better than participants l (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Mkhabela, Octavia Khabelani

title: Intercultural communication education and training goals, content, and methods
abstract: Using K. Krippendorff's (1980) content analysis procedures, a total of 260 college courses and professional training programs in intercultural communication from 9 cross-cultural education and training categories (intercultural communication, language and culture, international/global communication, human relations, interethnic/interracial, cultural diversity, multicultural education, cross-cultural psychology, and cross-cultural research) were analyzed on the basis of goals, content, and methods. A majority (88%) of both types of programs were judged as integrating multidimensional goals (cognitive, affective, and behavioral), content (culture general and culture specific) and process (intellectual and experiential). The results of the analysis suggest that while some practitioners still maintain a unidimensional focus in their cross-cultural training and education activities, the majority of them prefer teaching and learning strategies that are multidimensional. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Milhouse, Virginia H.

title: Teaching and the faculty role: Enhancing the commitment to instruction in American colleges and universities
abstract: Focuses on the role administrative action, socialization, and self-motivation play in shaping faculty behavior and teaching role. A model is introduced that examines 2 teaching-related outcomes: the percentage of time spent on teaching and instruction and the preferred amount of teaching. Data were gathered in the 1987–1988 National Survey of Postsecondary Faculty and included the section on full-time, tenure-track faculty in 4-yr institutions (n = 4,344) and on faculty ranked as assistant professors (n = 1,031). Findings revealed that faculty rewards dictated teaching and research time allocation, the importance of congruency between organizational culture and culture of orientation, intervention should begin in graduate school, and hours spent in class related positively to hours spent in teaching. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Fairweather, James S.; Rhoads, Robert A.

title: Perceptual learning in parafoveal vision
abstract: Tested the effects of practice on parafoveal vernier and resolution acuity in 20 college students, faculty, and staff. Task specificity, transfer of training to other retinal locations in the trained eye, and transfer of training to the untrained eye were measured to determine whether improvement on these tasks is the result of changes in the underlying physiological processes or simply the development of new cognitive strategies. Findings show that significant learning can occur for both vernier and resolution acuity in many individuals. There were significant individual differences in the degree and time–course of learning: learning transferred to the untrained task, and learning transferred to the other eye particularly when the visual pathway led to the trained hemisphere. Both physiological and cognitive processes may contribute to the improvement seen after repetitive practice on these tasks. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Beard, Bettina L.; Levi, Dennis M.; Reich, Lewis N.

title: The effects of metacognitive and metasocial processes on mathematical problem-solving skills
abstract: Two groups of Israeli college preparatory students were compared in their ability to solve algebra-rate problems using a computer program. One group received combined metacognitive/meta-affective skills training. The second group received only metacognitive training. Metacognitive skills that were trained included students' ability to regulate cognitive processes in a problem-solving situation. The meta-affective skills that were trained included students' ability to regulate affective processes in a problem-solving situation. It was predicted that the group that received the combined metacognitive and meta-affective skills training would outperform the group that received only the metacognitive skills training on: algebra-rate problems, meta-strategy knowledge, feelings of self control, and transfer. The study also examined the concept of metasociality. Metasociality was defined as the individuals' awareness of their social skills, ability to regulate these social skills, perceptions and beliefs and emotions with respect to another person, and the ways these beliefs and emotions affected social behavior in a dyadic problem-solving situation. There were no significant differences between the groups in pretest to postes in algebra-rate problems. Inconsistent with the hypothesis, the group with metacognitive skills training only showed significant superiority over the group with combined skills training for level of meta-strategy knowledge. Feelings of control in mathematical problem-solving situations were likely to improve in the metacognitive and meta-affective skills training group. No significant difference were found in transfer performance on algebra-motion problems. Content analysis revealed kinds of reactions during the problem-solving process: (a) the student was aware of the partner's contribution; (b) the student was aware only about the partner's presence; and (c) the student ignored the partner's presence. The study found that both interventions le (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Sherzer, Mordechai

title: Learning styles and adult intellectual development: An investigation of their influence on learning in a hypertext environment
abstract: The primary purpose of this study was to investigate influences of learning styles and the stages of adult intellectual development on learning in hypertext environments. A secondary purpose of the study was to determine the implications of these variables for the design of hypertext instruction. The four independent variables were: processing and perception dimensions of learning styles (as measured by Kolb's Learning Style Inventory (LSI)), adult intellectual development (as measured by the Learning Environment Preferences (LEP), an objective measure of Perry's Scheme of Intellectual and Ethical Development), and learner control. Learner control was defined through three hypertext structures which offered low (hierarchy structure), moderate (hierarchy with association structure), and high (web structure) levels of learner control. The dependent measures included an immediate posttest, delayed posttest, pre-belief questionnaire and post-belief questionnaire. Ninety-one undergraduate college students participated in the study. After completion of the initial instruments (LSI, LEP, pre-belief questionniare, and demographic survey) students were randomly assigned to one of three treatments representing the three levels of learner control. The topic of the instructional treatment was telecommunications. At the end of the lesson, students completed the immediate posttest and the post-belief questionnaire. A delayed posttest was administered two weeks later. Data analysis included the use of the General Linear Model, paired t-tests and simple ANOVAs. Performance results indicated that there was a significant three-way interaction among the factors of the processing dimension of learning styles, adult intellectual development, and learner control. There was a significant two-way interaction among the factors of the processing dimension of learning style and learner control. In addition, there were significant positive differences in each of the treatment groups for beli (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Rasmussen, Karen Lee

title: An evaluation of the VCU Mentoring Program
abstract: The goals of this study were as follows: (1) to conduct an implementation evaluation to assess the degree to which the VCU Mentoring Program was carried out as planned during the 1992-93 program year, (2) to conduct a summative evaluation to determine whether the VCU Mentoring Program met its immediate and intermediate objectives during the 1992-93 program year, and (3) to investigate whether variables including gender and attitudes towards race were associated with satisfaction with the mentoring relationship. Four sets of participants were utilized: (1) the treatment group consisting of thirty three African-American high school students who participated in the Mentoring program (mentees), (2) the parents of the high school student participants (N = 23), (3) twenty seven VCU college students who volunteered as mentors in the program, and (4) a comparison group consisting of 23 African-American high school students who did not participate in the Mentoring program. Results of the implementation evaluation indicated that the VCU Mentoring program did present all of its components. Workshop evaluations completed by the program participants indicated that the program did meet its immediate objectives for the 1992-93 program year. To investigate whether the program met its intermediate objectives during the 1992-93 program year, the treatment and comparison groups were tested before and after the program on relevant study variables including attitudes towards college, career maturity, study habits, expectations of college life, educational aspiration, grade point average and goal instability. The hypotheses that the treatment and comparison groups would differ significantly on the relevant study variables at the end of the program were not supported. Male mentees paired with female mentors reported significantly greater satisfaction with their mentoring relationships than mentees in same gender pairs. There was no significant relationship between attitudes towards race a (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Brooks, Leonie Jeannene

title: Essential learning contents in the curriculum for a certificate degree in personalized education for older adults
abstract: Outlines the steps needed to determine the contents of courses essential to a university program aimed at older adults returning to school to achieve a diploma. It is argued that course content should be aimed at developing the self-concept of the older adult and at fostering competency and achievement in work organization, working in groups, intellectual control, the acquisition of learning strategies, and continuing projects. Examples of courses in the program leading to a certificate degree in personalized education for older adults at the University of Quebec at Montreal are given as guidelines. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Lemieux, André

title: The generality vs domain-specificity of metacognitive skills in novice learning across domains
abstract: Examined the generality vs domain-specificity of the metacognitive skills that students of different levels of intelligence bring into new learning situations. Six relatively high and 8 relatively low intelligent college students (novices in the domains of physics and statistics) passed through 3 different simulation environments representing physics, statistics, and a fictitious domain. Both the S's metacognitive skillfulness and learning performances were assessed for each domain by analyzing their thinking aloud protocols. Results support the generality of novice metacognitive skills across domains. Furthermore, metacognitive skillfulness contributed to novice learning partly independently of intellectual ability. Implications for metacognitive skill training are discussed. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Veenman, Marcel V. J.; Elshout, Jan J.; Meijer, Joost

title: 'Learning style': Frameworks and instruments
abstract: In both education and training an important aspect of the design, development and delivery of learning is the role of individual differences between learners in terms of their 'learning styles.' Four broad categories of learning style have been identified: (1) cognitive personality elements; (2) information-processing style; (3) approaches to studying; and (4) instructional preferences. A study of 245 business studies undergraduates (aged 18–58 yrs) aimed to describe the range of individual differences present within the sample; investigate the relationship between learners' cognitive styles, learning styles, approaches to studying, and learning preferences; and consider the implications of learning style for teaching and learning in higher education. No statistically significant correlations were found between cognitive style, as measured by the Cognitive Styles Analysis, and any of the other style constructs used. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)
author: Sadler-Smith, Eugene

title: Effects of counseling on grades and retention
